measurement.happened:
This week in Japan was dominated by a landmark monetary policy shift, a tangle of diplomatic and defense agreements, and a series of corporate and political dramas that together painted a picture of a country navigating its post-deflation era while juggling relationships with both allies and rivals.

The single biggest story was the Bank of Japan's decision on October 30. The BOJ held rates but explicitly declared that Japan's inflation trend has reached the 2 percent target it has chased for over a decade, and it guided markets toward further tightening, with analysts and the WSJ both framing it as clearing the way for a December rate hike. Trend inflation hit a three-year high, business service prices accelerated, and the FT and Bloomberg both noted the end of Japan's cheap-money era. The yen's role in the Latin American carry trade withstood a Brazil rout, and Japanese bonds were steady ahead of the decision, supported by a strong auction. Moody's saw a positive shift in growth. In short, the BOJ's hawkish pause sent a clear signal: the deflation era is officially over, and the next move is up. This is the headline that will define Japanese economic policy for the next several months.

On the diplomatic and defense front, Japan signed off on a joint US-Japanese facility for missile production, a deal the WSJ framed as the US turning to Japan as its own stockpiles dwindle and China looms. Chancellor Merz visited Japan and invited it to back a broader trade alliance while weighing Germany's role in the GCAP fighter jet program, with China asking Germany to be rational. Japan also pushed to remove Myanmar from a global financial watchdog's blacklist, and the US, South Korea, and Japan jointly called for complete denuclearisation of North Korea after Pyongyang fired a dozen ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan. Japan demanded the release of a Japanese national in a meeting with Lavrov, and Deutsche Welle noted the arrest of a Japanese journalist by Russia as another sign of deteriorating ties. The overall picture is a Japan actively deepening its security and trade architecture with the West while managing an increasingly prickly relationship with China.

The Japan-China relationship produced the week's most colourful cultural story: Sanrio, the Hello Kitty company, scrapped a Japanese TV tie-up after Chinese fans and officials took offence, and the BBC, FT, Bloomberg, and TV5Monde all covered the episode. China's Xi called on Japan to protect the political foundation of bilateral ties. Chinese EVs are proving a rougher road in Japan than in South Korea, and Chinese carmakers overtook Japan in Europe for the first time. A Chinese student was arrested in Tokyo over a May pepper-spray attack. And Bloomberg ran a piece on whether Chinamaxxing is about to reach its Made-in-Japan moment. The relationship is clearly more competitive and more emotionally charged than a year ago.

Domestic politics and the imperial succession law also generated significant coverage. The revised Imperial House law, which reinforces male-only succession, took effect on October 24, and a cartoonist immediately took it to court over the male-only heirs provision. Former Prime Minister Yasuo Fukuda, a known proponent of ties with China, died at 90, and a Reuters podcast explored how PM Takaichi's success may backfire on Japan. A proposed consumption tax cut was called bad economics but good populism by one economist. The political mood is one of cautious populism meeting the new reality of higher inflation.

Cybersecurity was a prominent theme. The Reuters headline noted Japanese companies compensating users as cyberattacks buffet the economy. Bloomberg reported a surge in cyberattacks testing Japan's push to strengthen defenses. The WSJ covered a GMO hack hitting forex brokers, and the PM promised a prompt reaction. Japan is clearly feeling the pain of a new wave of digital intrusions and is responding with both rhetoric and policy.

The corporate world had its share of drama. Nidec announced it would sue its own founder over his role in what the FT called Japan's biggest accounting fraud in a decade. EQT and Bain launched a five-billion-dollar showdown over Kakaku, heralding a contested Japan buyout era. Tokyo Electron's outlook beat expectations on surging AI chip spending. Toyota and Waymo announced plans to test autonomous bZ4X vehicles in Japan in 2027. Takeda will seek approval for a gastric cancer drug next year. Omron is targeting India for manufacturing. And Japan is scaling back fuel subsidies as costs from the Iran war mount, while also planning to tap US crude imports for energy security.

In the sports world, the Tokyo WTA Open was a marquee event: Rybakina secured the year-end number one ranking before withdrawing with a neck injury, Osaka was knocked out by teenager Pohankova in the second round in front of home fans, and Leylah Fernandez advanced to the final before Shnaider won the title. In rugby, Wales completed a double over Japan in the WXV Global Series, recording a 17-0 shutout in Tokyo. Japanese golfer Yuri Yoshida won her first LPGA title. Pitcher Kaima Taira is set to move to MLB. A FIFA official from Japan resigned over the Infantino re-election row. And a 90-year-old Japanese bodybuilder flexed on a Spanish stage, which Reuters covered with a smile.

In culture and mourning, manga legend Tetsuya Chiba, creator of Ashita no Joe, died at 87. Tokyo hosted a yokai-themed Halloween parade. A festival blessed kimono-clad pets in a town lacking enough children. And travelers could still experience Edo-period culture, CNN noted.

Weather-wise, Tropical Storm Champi battered Japan after hitting Taiwan, though it did not appear to cause catastrophic damage by the end of the week.

Alaska Airlines announced nonstop service between Anchorage and Tokyo Narita, a small but symbolic step in trans-Pacific connectivity.
measurement.expected:
In the week from November 1 to roughly November 8, 2026, I expect the following developments in Japan.

BOJ aftermath and market digestion. Almost certain: Japanese financial markets will spend the first few trading days digesting the BOJ's hawkish guidance. The yen will likely strengthen modestly against the dollar as carry-trade positions are unwound, and Japanese government bond yields will edge higher. Analysts and fund managers will publish follow-up notes, and the conversation will shift from whether the BOJ will hike to when exactly, with December being the dominant guess. The FT, Bloomberg, and CNBC will run a steady stream of commentary. I am almost certain this will be the week's top economic story.

Japan-China friction continues. Probable: The Hello Kitty/Sanrio TV drama will not resolve overnight. Expect follow-up reporting, possibly a statement from Sanrio or the Japanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and at least one or two more small cultural or commercial spillovers as Chinese social media keeps the issue alive. The broader narrative of Chinese carmakers overtaking Japan in Europe and Chinese EVs struggling domestically will generate more trade-policy commentary. I rate continued low-level diplomatic friction as probable, with a full-blown trade spat as possible but not the base case.

US-Japan defense and missile production. Probable: The joint missile production facility deal will move into implementation planning. Expect statements from the Ministry of Defense, possibly a press conference in Sana or Futenma, and coverage of where exactly the facility will be sited. The Okinawa angle will keep the US Marine indictment in the news: the indicted Marine's legal team will file motions, and Okinawan local politicians will use the case to press for a base reduction. I rate a visible Okinawa protest or at least a council statement as probable.

North Korea and the Sea of Japan. Possible: After the dozen ballistic missiles fired on October 29, Japan will likely conduct or announce joint exercises with the US and South Korea within the next week. The trilateral denuclearisation statement will be referenced in diplomatic briefings. I rate a new North Korean missile test in this exact week as possible but not certain, and I would not bet on a major escalation.

Imperial succession law and court case. Possible: The cartoonist's lawsuit will see its first procedural steps or media briefings. Public debate will continue, with opinion pieces in the Asahi, Yomiuri, and NHK. I rate a high-profile public hearing as unlikely in this specific week, but a steady drumbeat of commentary as probable.

Cybersecurity policy. Probable: Following the PM's promise of a prompt reaction, the government will likely announce or leak details of a new cybersecurity fund, a draft bill, or an expanded mandate for the National Cybersecurity Center. The GMO forex broker hack will generate at least one more follow-up story. I rate a concrete policy announcement as probable.

Nidec fraud and corporate governance. Possible: The lawsuit against the founder will see its first court filings or a joint press statement. The Kakaku buyout war between EQT and Bain will enter a bidding or due-diligence phase with more analyst coverage. I rate a major corporate headline as possible.

Sports and culture. Almost certain: J1 League matches will continue (Fagiano Okayama vs Tokyo, V-Varen Nagasaki vs Tokyo Verdy were already scheduled). Post-tournament coverage of the WTA Tokyo Open and the WXV rugby series will fill sports pages. The 90-year-old bodybuilder and the pet-blessing festival will generate light cultural pieces. I am almost certain sports and culture will occupy a steady share of the news cycle.

Energy and fuel. Possible: With Japan scaling back fuel subsidies and planning US crude imports, the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry will likely issue technical guidance or a public consultation. The floating offshore wind project with Siemens Energy will see a follow-up announcement or site survey news. I rate a policy paper or presser as possible.

Takaichi government and consumption tax. Possible: The proposed consumption tax cut will generate a round of cabinet discussion or a leaked policy paper. The Reuters podcast on Takaichi's success potentially backfiring will be echoed in domestic media. I rate a cabinet-level statement as possible.

Less likely surprises: A second major cyberattack on a Japanese financial institution within this exact week (possible but would be a big story). A sudden yen flash-move of more than 2 percent triggered by a US data release (possible). A North Korean submarine or missile incident in the Seto Inland Sea (unlikely but not impossible). A surprise BOJ communication or emergency meeting (unlikely). A major earthquake (always possible, never predictable).

Things I would not bet on: A snap election or cabinet reshuffle in this one-week window. A full-scale trade war declaration between Japan and China. A new prime minister. A major natural disaster (typhoon, earthquake, volcano) in this specific week, though the Japanese archipelago never makes it impossible. A BOJ emergency rate cut reversing the hawkish signal. A constitutional amendment vote. A major oil spill or shipping-lane closure in the Strait of Malacca affecting Japan's imports. A second Nidec-scale accounting fraud being revealed in the same week.

Japan signed a joint US missile production facility, deepened the GCAP fighter jet conversation with Germany, and pushed a trilateral denuclearisation statement, making diplomacy and defense pacts the week's second major thread.

From the Hello Kitty TV drama igniting a China backlash, to Nidec suing its own founder over a decade's worst accounting fraud, to a FIFA official resigning and the imperial succession law being challenged in court, the week was thick with corporate and political drama.

delta.motion:
The most dramatic growth between the two photographs is in Japan's security architecture with the West. A week ago the US-Japan defense thread was a mix of a BYD ban at an air base, joint drills disrupted by a typhoon, and secret talks with Myanmar's military rulers. By the second week, Japan had signed off on a joint US-Japanese missile production facility, Chancellor Merz had visited to discuss the GCAP fighter jet and a broader trade alliance, and the three allies had jointly demanded North Korea's complete denuclearisation after Pyongyang fired a dozen ballistic missiles. The thread went from a series of small irritants to a structural deepening of the alliance, and the speed was fast: the missile facility and the Merz visit both landed within the same week. The Japan-China relationship also grew in emotional intensity. It moved from a diplomatic grumble over the Yasukuni Shrine to a full cultural blow-up when Sanrio scrapped a TV tie-up because Chinese fans and officials took offence, and to Xi personally calling on Japan to protect the political foundation of bilateral ties. A Chinese student was arrested in Tokyo over a pepper-spray incident, and Chinese EVs were described as hitting a rougher road in Japan than in Korea. The friction went from state-to-state to pop-culture and street-level.

The BOJ story grew from an expected decision to an actual one. In the first photograph the policy meeting was still ahead, and the narrative was about signals, board-member comments, and market pricing. In the second photograph the meeting had happened: the BOJ held rates, declared inflation at target, and pointed firmly toward a December hike. The 'end of cheap money' framing is a step beyond what the first week's headlines suggested, and it shifted the entire fiscal and corporate conversation. Fuel subsidies moved from 'Japan weighs phasing out' to 'Japan is scaling back fuel subsidies as Iran war costs mount,' and a new thread about tapping US crude imports appeared. The corporate world grew from a steady drumbeat of trade data and chip exports into a cluster of dramatic stories: Nidec suing its own founder over what the FT called Japan's biggest accounting fraud in a decade, EQT and Bain launching a five-billion-dollar Kakaku showdown, and Toyota partnering with Waymo on autonomous bZ4X vehicles. The cyber thread also grew in scope. The first week's PHP vulnerabilities and GMO hack became a broader narrative of Japanese companies compensating users as cyberattacks buffet the economy, with the PM personally promising a prompt reaction.

Several themes shrank or faded. The Mars mission, which dominated the first week as a historic first, dropped almost entirely from the second week's headlines. The probe is in transit, but the novelty has worn off and no new JAXA press conference or technical drama made the cut. Typhoon Champi went from a major disruption story with flight cancellations and disrupted US-Japan drills to a single line noting it battered Japan after hitting Taiwan, with no mention of catastrophic damage. The trade deficit from soaring oil imports and the rare-earth supply squeeze from China, both prominent in the first week, receded from the headlines. The Fiji rugby result, which generated two TV5Monde stories, was replaced by Wales completing a double over Japan with a 17-0 shutout, and the Asian Cup uncertainty that had been simmering lost some of its urgency. The Daiichi Life/Challenger offer, the Tiffany's Japan building price cut, and the Natixis advisory acquisition all vanished from the second week's coverage.

New themes appeared that had no counterpart in the first photograph. The Imperial House succession law taking effect and a cartoonist immediately challenging the male-only provision in court is a fresh domestic political story. Former PM Yasuo Fukuda's death at 90 added a layer of political mourning and reflection. A proposed consumption tax cut was described as bad economics but good populism. The North Korea missile launch, a dozen ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan, is a new regional security event that was not present in the first week. The Merz visit and the GCAP discussion open a Germany-Japan axis that was not in the first photograph. The Alaska Airlines nonstop Anchorage-Tokyo route is a small but new signal of trans-Pacific connectivity. The Sanrio/Hello Kitty scandal is a new cultural flashpoint. The Nidec fraud and the Kakaku buyout war are new corporate dramas. Tetsuya Chiba's death at 87, the yokai Halloween parade, and the pet-blessing festival are new cultural and human-interest items. The FIFA official resignation over the Infantino re-election row is a new sports-governance story. The Toyota-Waymo autonomous driving partnership and the Takeda gastric cancer drug approval are new tech and pharma threads. The overall impression is that the second week is broader, more dramatic in its corporate and cultural stories, and more structurally significant in its security and monetary policy developments, while the first week's sense of a single dominant story (the Mars launch) has dispersed into multiple parallel threads.
delta.wind:
The BOJ prediction was almost exactly right. The expectation was a hawkish hold with a clear signal of a December hike, and that is precisely what happened on October 30. The 25-to-30 percent chance of an actual rate hike at this meeting was correctly judged as unlikely. The one place the expectation undershot was in the framing: the BOJ did not just hold and hint; it explicitly declared that trend inflation has reached the 2 percent target, which is a more definitive statement than 'raising the inflation forecast.' The market reaction was steadier than the expectation of volatility around the press conference suggested, with bonds supported by a strong auction. The 'end of cheap money' language from the FT and Bloomberg goes slightly beyond what the first week's signals implied, but the direction was correct.

The Takaichi and cabinet politics prediction was partly right and partly off. The expectation of a concrete policy move on energy subsidies was confirmed: Japan is scaling back fuel subsidies and considering a consumption tax cut. However, the cabinet scandal that was mentioned in the first week seems to have faded rather than triggering a reshuffle, and no major reshuffle was announced. The weak yen and high-rates headache was addressed more through the BOJ decision and the broader fiscal conversation than through a specific Takaichi press conference. The Fukuda death and the 'Takaichi success may backfire' podcast add a reflective political dimension that was not in the expectation. The consumption tax cut proposal, described as bad economics but good populism, is a new thread that fits the 'cautious populism' tone but was not specifically predicted.

The Typhoon Champi aftermath prediction was directionally right but overestimated the story's persistence. The expectation was that damage assessments and disrupted schedules would dominate the first few days. In reality, the storm is mentioned only briefly in the second week as having battered Japan, with no major damage story, no insurance-claims cycle, and no rescheduled-drills follow-up. The US-Japan drills disruption faded quickly. The typhoon was a one-week news cycle, as predicted, but even shorter than the expectation implied.

The BYD ban and US-Japan-China friction prediction was partly right in direction but the specific BYD thread faded faster than expected. The expectation was a few more headlines, a BYD statement, and a China diplomatic reaction tied to Yasukuni. In reality, the BYD ban dropped from the headlines, and the China reaction came through a different channel entirely: the Sanrio/Hello Kitty scandal and Xi's personal call on Japan. The US-Japan defense thread grew much faster and more structurally than predicted, with the missile production facility and the Merz/GCAP visit, neither of which was in the expectation. The secret US-Myanmar talks evolved into Japan pushing to remove Myanmar from a financial watchdog's blacklist, which is a different and more concrete outcome than the expectation of follow-up reporting.

The cyber and tech prediction was right in scope but understated in intensity. The expectation was bank and airline status updates and an FSA statement. The reality is broader: Japanese companies are compensating users, the GMO hack hit forex brokers specifically, and the PM personally promised a prompt reaction. The 'cyberattacks buffet the economy' framing from Reuters is more severe than the first week's 'scrambled to patch' language. The AI chip export boom continued, with Tokyo Electron beating expectations, which is consistent. The rare-earth squeeze from China, expected to generate at least one more headline, did not make the second week's cut, which is a small miss.

The Mars mission prediction was correct in content but the story's prominence was overestimated. The expectation was regular updates, a JAXA press conference, and sustained public interest. In reality, the mission is in transit but has largely dropped from the headlines. No JAXA press conference or technical issue made the second week's coverage. The novelty wore off faster than expected.

The sports prediction was partly right. The Japan Open was covered, but the narrative was different: Shnaider won the title, not Boulter, and Osaka lost early in front of home fans, which is a more dramatic and locally resonant story than the expectation of a straightforward final. The Fiji rugby result was replaced by Wales completing a double, which is a bigger story for Japanese rugby fans. The Asian Cup uncertainty simmered but did not produce the specific headlines expected. The Infantino row generated a FIFA official resignation, which is a concrete outcome not in the expectation. The Ikeda doping clearance did not reappear. The Yuri Yoshida LPGA win and the Kaima Taira MLB move are new sports threads not in the prediction.

The fiscal and energy prediction was right. The government did finalize its position on energy subsidies, scaling them back, and the trade deficit from oil imports remained relevant through the Iran war angle. The new thread about tapping US crude imports for energy security was not in the expectation but fits the broader energy-security narrative.

The 'less likely surprises' list was mostly right in its probabilities. The sudden BOJ rate hike (15-20 percent) did not happen. The dramatic Japan-China diplomatic exchange (10-15 percent) happened in a different form: the Sanrio scandal and Xi's call are more cultural than diplomatic, but they are a form of the expected friction. The second cyber incident (10 percent) did happen, with the GMO forex broker hit and the broader wave. The surprise cabinet reshuffle (10-15 percent) did not happen. The Mars probe technical issue (5-10 percent) did not happen. The list of 'things I would not bet on' was mostly correct: no full trade war, no major earthquake, no Diet legislative breakthrough, no sudden break in Japan-Russia ties (the journalist is still jailed, confirmed by DW), no major corporate bankruptcy (the Nidec fraud is close but is a lawsuit, not a bankruptcy), no BOJ governor change, and no vote of no confidence. The one item that came closer to the 'not betting on' list than expected is the North Korea missile launch, which is a significant regional security event that was not in either the expectation or the 'not betting on' list, and it reshaped the US-Japan-China security conversation within the week.

The overall pattern of misses is that the expectation was too focused on the specific threads that were already in the headlines (BYD, Mars, typhoon, Fiji) and not enough on the structural and diplomatic developments that were building underneath them (the missile facility, the Merz visit, the North Korea launch, the Sanrio scandal, the corporate fraud stories). The expectation correctly identified the BOJ and the energy-subsidy threads but underestimated the speed at which the security architecture would deepen and the cultural friction with China would escalate. The expectation also overestimated the persistence of one-week stories (typhoon, Mars, BYD) and underestimated the emergence of new one-week stories (Sanrio, Nidec, North Korea, Merz). This suggests that for Japan, the forecasting model should weight structural diplomatic and corporate developments more heavily than the specific headline items of the prior week, because the headline items change fast while the underlying tensions build slowly and then surface in unexpected forms.
delta.driver: The force pushing Japan from the first photograph to the second is the collision of three slow-burning processes that all reached a tipping point in the same eight-day window. The first is the end of the deflation era. The BOJ's explicit declaration that inflation has hit target, the fuel-subsidy retreat, the consumption-tax-cut proposal, the Nidec accounting fraud, and the Tokyo Electron beat all point to a Japanese economy that is no longer in the low-price, low-growth, low-interest regime it inhabited for two decades, and every institution, corporation, and household is now re-pricing itself into the new reality. The second is the security realignment. The US needs missile production capacity as its own stockpiles dwindle, Germany wants a GCAP partner, North Korea is firing a dozen missiles a week, and China is getting louder culturally and diplomatically. Japan is being pulled into a more explicit and more industrialized Western security architecture, and the missile facility, the Merz visit, and the joint denuclearisation demand are all symptoms of that pull. The third is the domestic political and cultural reckoning. The Imperial succession law taking effect, the Fukuda death, the Sanrio scandal, the Nidec fraud, the consumption-tax populism, and the Takaichi 'success may backfire' narrative all reflect a country that is simultaneously trying to modernize its institutions, mourn its old guard, and manage a population that is increasingly sensitive to both external provocation and internal corruption. These three forces are not independent: the higher-inflation reality makes the fiscal cost of the security build-up more painful, the security build-up raises the political stakes of the fiscal choices, and the domestic cultural friction with China makes every security decision feel like a civilizational choice. The speed at which all three arrived in the same week is what makes the second photograph look so different from the first, even though the underlying trends were visible in both.

SPORTS AND CULTURE (lower confidence in specific items, higher confidence in the general pattern): The WTA Japan Open is over, and the next major tennis event is a week or two away, so tennis will be a lighter story. The Wales-versus-Japan rugby result will generate a follow-up: a squad announcement for the next match, a coaching change discussion, or a fan reaction piece. LESS LIKELY SURPRISES THE MOTION MAKES MORE PROBABLE: A second North Korea missile launch within the week (25 to 30 percent, up from the base rate because of the cluster pattern and the joint denuclearisation demand). A Chinese state-media or ministry reaction specifically to the missile production facility (20 to 25 percent, up from the base rate because the deal is industrial and China has been reacting through industrial channels). WHAT I WOULD NOT BET ON: A BOJ rate hike this week (the decision was October 30, the next meeting is December, and the hold was explicit). A cabinet reshuffle or a second ministerial resignation. crystal.eli5:
Japan just got a big announcement from its central bank: prices are finally rising at the rate the bank has been aiming for, and the era of really cheap loans is officially over. That means businesses and the government have to rethink how they borrow money and spend it, and there is already a fight brewing between the bank (which wants to keep prices in check) and the government (which wants to cut taxes and keep subsidies going). Expect a few days of markets going up and down as everyone figures out what this means.

At the same time, Japan and the United States just agreed to build missiles together on Japanese soil, and a German leader visited to talk about making fighter jets as a team. This is a big deal because it means Japan is becoming a bigger part of the Western security machine, and China is going to notice. There is also a chance North Korea fires off more missiles this week, because they have a habit of doing that in clusters.

On the home front, things are a bit messy. A big company is suing its own founder for cooking the books, two private-equity firms are fighting over another company, hackers have been hitting Japanese businesses, and a cartoonist is taking the government to court over a new law about who can be emperor. A beloved manga artist and a former prime minister both died, which gives everyone a moment to look back. It is a busy, complicated week, but nothing is on fire. The big story is that Japan is adjusting to a new economic reality while simultaneously building a bigger security role, and everyone is still figuring out how those two things fit together.

judgment.reading_a:

The sports calls (WTA Japan Open, Infantino, Fiji rugby) mostly landed, though the big rugby story was actually Wales' 17-0 shutout rather than Fiji. The Japan-Russia journalist thread was correctly flagged. The typhoon aftermath was right, though less dramatic than A implied. What A missed or under-weighted: The Hello Kitty/Sanrio China drama was one of the week's most colorful and widely covered stories (six or more headlines across BBC, FT, Bloomberg, TV5Monde, AFP), and A did not mention it at all. Chancellor Merz's visit and the GCAP fighter jet discussion were absent. North Korea's ballistic missile launches and the trilateral denuclearisation call were not mentioned. What A expected that did not come: A expected 'parliamentary questions on whether the government's cyber preparedness was adequate' and 'a minor reshuffle or a ministerial comment' for the cabinet scandal, neither of which clearly appeared. The 'disrupted joint island drills may be rescheduled' was not a visible headline. A's low-confidence calls on a second typhoon, a Japan-Russia breakthrough, a full cabinet resignation, and a second Mars spike were all correctly absent.

Overall, A's picture was directionally correct on the major economic and political axes but narrower in scope than the week's actual breadth. It captured the spine of the week (BOJ, Takaichi pressure, cyber, China friction, sports) but missed several of the week's most distinctive and widely covered stories, particularly the cultural-diplomatic ones (Hello Kitty, Merz, North Korea) and the corporate drama.

judgment.comparison:
Both forecasts got the spine of the week right: the BOJ hawkish hold as the dominant story, Takaichi under pressure, the cyber/GMO hack thread, China friction, sports (WTA, rugby), the typhoon aftermath, the Mars drip, and the Russia simmer. Neither was dramatically wrong on the big picture, and both correctly avoided over-betting on structural breaks (no rate hike, no cabinet crisis, no second typhoon, no Japan-Russia breakthrough).

Where they diverge is in specificity and structure. A offered a more vivid narrative, and its 'Takaichi versus the BOJ' framing and 'one-year reality check' were prescient and resonated with the week's coverage. A's specific mentions of the Rengo settlement, the GMO hack by name, and the GlobalFoundries bet showed granular knowledge, though the GlobalFoundries and several corporate calls (Tiffany's, Natixis, Daiichi Life/Challenger) did not clearly surface. A's 'Asian Para Games anthem mix-up' was not evident.

B was more systematic and gave explicit probability ranges, which is more useful for a reader trying to calibrate expectations. B's Myanmar call and Fiji rugby call both landed, while A's equivalent corporate and cultural calls were more mixed. B's 'surprises' section was a practical tool: the diplomatic exchange (Hello Kitty, Xi) and the cyber follow-up both appeared in the 10-15 percent range B assigned, while the items B put at 5-10 percent (Mars technical issue) and 15-20 percent (surprise rate hike) did not materialize. B's 'things I would not bet on' list was comprehensive and accurate.

Both missed the same cluster of distinctive stories: the Hello Kitty/Sanrio China drama, the US-Japan missile production facility, Chancellor Merz's visit and GCAP, North Korea's missile launches, the Imperial succession law, the deaths of Fukuda and Chiba, and the Nidec/EQT-Bain corporate drama. These omissions are the main reason neither forecast fully captured the week's breadth.

On balance, B served a reader marginally better. Its structure made it easier to scan and prioritize. Its explicit probabilities gave a clearer sense of what was likely versus unlikely. Its specific calls that landed (Myanmar, Fiji, the gasoline subsidy, the cyber status updates) were slightly more numerous than A's equivalent specific calls. A's narrative vividness and the 'Takaichi versus the BOJ' framing were valuable, but B's broader diplomatic coverage and practical probability ranges made it the more useful document for someone trying to anticipate the week's shape. The difference is small; both were strong forecasts that captured the dominant story and the major themes.
